Keep values as the supplied list; write the function, comma-separated return pair and the assignment unpacking bounds(values) into smallest and largest.

solution_files.content:
_input_first = 3
first = _input_first
second = 8
third = 5
values = [first, second, third]
def bounds(values):
    return min(values), max(values)
smallest, largest = bounds(values)

spec.expr:
(lambda scope: (exec('import ast
tree = ast.parse(open("main.py").read())
_skill_ok = any(isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == "bounds" and any(isinstance(r, ast.Return) and isinstance(r.value, ast.Tuple) for r in ast.walk(n)) for n in tree.body) and any(isinstance(n, ast.Assign) and any(isinstance(t, ast.Tuple) and [x.id for x in t.elts] == ["smallest", "largest"] for t in n.targets) for n in tree.body)
', scope), ([type(bounds(values)).__name__, bounds(values), smallest, largest]) if scope["_skill_ok"] else None)[1])(globals().copy())

blocks.text: Use the ordinary order fee unless a call overrides it.
In def name(required, optional=default):, omitting optional at a call uses its default.
Positional arguments bind in order; keyword arguments bind by parameter name. Keywords follow ordinary positional arguments.
Supply required arguments. Do not bind a parameter twice or use an unaccepted keyword.
Identify quantity and price as required parameters and fee as defaulted. Compare omitting fee, naming all arguments, and using keywords after positional arguments. A named fee overrides the default.

public.prompt: Define cost(quantity, price, fee=2) to return quantity * price + fee. Call it once using only keyword arguments with fee=5, and once omitting fee to use its default. Assign each returned value to a variable. Use quantity_input and price_input at both calls. Store the explicit keyword-call result in with_fee and the call omitting fee in default_cost. solution_files.content:
quantity_input = 3
price_input = 4
def cost(quantity, price, fee=2):
    return quantity * price + fee
with_fee = cost(quantity=quantity_input, price=price_input, fee=5)
default_cost = cost(quantity_input, price_input)

spec.expr:
(lambda scope: (exec('import ast
tree = ast.parse(open("main.py").read())
_skill_ok = any(isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == "cost" and bool(n.args.defaults) for n in tree.body) and any(isinstance(n, ast.Assign) and isinstance(n.value, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.value.func, ast.Name) and n.value.func.id == "cost" and not n.value.args and {k.arg for k in n.value.keywords} == {"quantity", "price", "fee"} for n in tree.body) and any(isinstance(n, ast.Assign) and isinstance(n.value, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.value.func, ast.Name) and n.value.func.id == "cost" and len(n.value.args) == 2 and not n.value.keywords for n in tree.body)
', scope), ([with_fee, default_cost]) if scope["_skill_ok"] else None)[1])(globals().copy())

blocks.text: Distinguish the module quantity from a helper’s local quantity.
Names assigned within a function are local throughout that function unless declared otherwise. Reading a local before binding it raises UnboundLocalError.
Without a local binding, ordinary lookup can read an enclosing or module binding.
globals() returns the current module namespace dictionary. globals()["name"] explicitly reads that entry even when a local shadows it.
Ordinary local assignment changes the local binding, not a same-named module binding.
A global declaration directs assignments to that name’s module binding instead.

blocks.code:
quantity = 3

def show():
    quantity = 5
    print(quantity)
    print(globals()["quantity"])

show()
print(quantity)

annotations.text: The unindented assignment binds the module name.
This assignment binds a separate local quantity.
Explicit lookup selects the module namespace entry.

blocks.text: In show, ordinary quantity reads its local binding, while globals()["quantity"] reads the module entry. After the call, the module quantity still refers to its module binding.
A module quantity cannot rescue a read of an unbound local quantity. Assignment makes that name local throughout the function unless declared otherwise.

options.text: (1) can read the module binding; (2) explicitly reads the module binding; (3) raises UnboundLocalError
All three ordinary reads use the module binding

a.message: Without a local assignment, (1) can read the module binding. globals()["quantity"] explicitly accesses that binding in (2). The later assignment makes quantity local throughout (3), so reading it before it is bound raises UnboundLocalError.

b.message: (2) uses an explicit globals() lookup, not an ordinary local read. In (3), the later assignment makes quantity local, and the earlier unbound read raises UnboundLocalError.

c.message: (1) can read the module binding because it does not assign a local quantity. (2) explicitly reads the module binding through globals(). (3) reads an unbound local name and raises UnboundLocalError.

public.prompt: Write show() so it reads the module-level quantity through globals()["quantity"], assigns that value to a local quantity, increases the local quantity by 2, and returns it without changing the module-level quantity. Write the function body yourself, then assign the result of show() to result.

allowed_syntax: def show(): with an indented function body

solution_files.content:
quantity = 3
def show():
    quantity = globals()["quantity"]
    quantity = quantity + 2
    return quantity
result = show()

spec.expr:
(lambda scope: (exec('import ast
tree = ast.parse(open("main.py").read())
_skill_ok = any(isinstance(n, ast.FunctionDef) and n.name == "show" and any(isinstance(a, ast.Assign) and isinstance(a.value, ast.Subscript) and isinstance(a.value.value, ast.Call) and isinstance(a.value.value.func, ast.Name) and a.value.value.func.id == "globals" for a in n.body) for n in tree.body)
', scope), ([result, quantity]) if scope["_skill_ok"] else None)[1])(globals().copy())

Ordinary quantity can refer to a local; globals()["quantity"] explicitly reads the module entry.

An assignment to quantity anywhere in an ordinary function body makes quantity local throughout that function unless declared otherwise. Reading it before that local assignment binds it raises UnboundLocalError; a module-level quantity does not supply a fallback.
